source.title: Interpreting the Second-Order Effects of Neurons in CLIP
source.authors: Yossi Gandelsman; Alexei A. Efros; Jacob Steinhardt

record.tranche_reason: It measures whether a neuron’s second-order effect in CLIP is well approximated by a single direction, using PCA and downstream accuracy rather than the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports neuron polysemy, adversarial-image results, and segmentation results. Those do not test whether polysemanticity is caused by limited capacity, whether SAE features are canonical units, or the toy-model superposition account. Cited claims from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper's core results characterise CLIP neurons' second-order effects. Those effects are concentrated in late layers, sparse across images, and approximately rank-1. The paper then decomposes each effect direction into text descriptions. A neuron's output-effect direction being rank-1 is not a test of whether features are 1-D (V6). The single direction is itself polysemantic, decomposing into many unrelated concepts, so it is a neuron-level construct, not a feature. Polysemanticity is shown only qualitatively, in a vision model rather than an LLM. It is then exploited as a tool for semantic adversarial examples. No capacity, toy-model, SAE or feature-dimensionality test is run.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. The authors find second-order effects significant only for under 2% of images and approximately rank-1. They decompose each effect into sparse text sets that reveal polysemantic neurons, which they read as neurons behaving as a superposition of features. They exploit this to mass-produce semantic adversarial images and to do zero-shot segmentation. The polysemanticity claim rests on qualitative examples; no capacity or causal account is tested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a second-order effect analysis, PCA, and text-based sparse decomposition on CLIP neurons, rather than training and measuring toy networks with superposed sparse features.
record.method_sensitivity: The magnitude of second-order ablation effects varies by layer; the largest drops in ViT-B-32 occur in layers 8–10. For ViT-L-14, the maximal drop is smaller and spread across more layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Each CLIP neuron's second-order effect is approximately rank-1. PC1 explains 48.2 of the variance vs 11.0 for the indirect effect (layer 9). PC1 reconstruction gives a negligible accuracy drop across layers in ViT-B-32, with a similar pattern in ViT-L-14.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual neuron contributions to a model's output, routed through later attention, are approximately one-dimensional in output space.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse text decompositions (m=128) of neuron effect directions, and the neurons' top images, show neurons writing toward unrelated concepts (e.g. yacht and cabriolet). The evidence is qualitative only (Table 2, Fig 5, Fig 13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons in vision-language models (CLIP) are polysemantic in their output effects.

record.problems: The study does not directly test feature competition or capacity pressure. The first-PC variance result is 48.2, and the reconstruction accuracy values are only shown in a figure without exact values. ViT-L-14 results use 10% of ImageNet validation data.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. The paper’s adversarial-image and segmentation outcomes concern applications of its interpretation method, not the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity transitions or geometry.
No test of capacity pressure or importance-based allocation.
Polysemantic neurons are reported, but their cause is not tested.
No LLMs and no SAEs. Polysemanticity is shown only qualitatively in CLIP vision neurons.
Feature dimensionality is not measured; only the rank of neuron second-order effects is measured.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link conflates a neuron's rank-1 output effect with 1-D features. The paper itself says that one direction carries multiple concepts, so the result says nothing about feature dimensionality. The adversarial and segmentation results are applications and are rightly left out. The qualitative CLIP polysemanticity evidence might matter if the collection adds a vision analogue of V4.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and feature importance.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or causes important features to receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
The paper reports polysemantic neurons but does not test whether they arise without capacity pressure or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
LLM feature distribution across neurons and recovery of sparse features in LLMs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.
The paper measures the dimensionality of CLIP neuron second-order effects, not the dimensionality of features in a toy-model superposition setting.

rows.subject: OpenAI’s ViT-B-32 CLIP
rows.operation_detail: Measured the variance explained by the first principal component of neuron effects.
rows.measure: Variance explained by first principal component
rows.note: The second-order effect has substantially more variance in its first principal component than the indirect effect, but the reported 48.2 does not by itself indicate that nearly all variance is one-dimensional.
rows.check: Measures variance explained by PC1 of a neuron's second-order effect (48.2 vs 11.0 for indirect effect, layer 9, ViT-B-32). That is the dimensionality of a neuron's output contribution, not of a superposed feature, so it does not bear on V6. The value is presumably a percentage; units are not stated in Table 1.

rows.subject: OpenAI’s ViT-B-32 CLIP
rows.operation_detail: Replaced each neuron’s second-order effect with its first-principal-component approximation and evaluated ImageNet classification accuracy.
rows.measure: Zero-shot ImageNet classification accuracy after first-PC reconstruction
rows.note: The text says replacement with the first-PC approximation causes a negligible drop from the baseline. Exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Rank-1 reconstruction of a neuron's second-order effect gives a 'negligible drop' in accuracy (Fig 3, figure only). This is a neuron-level output-effect property, and the paper says the direction mixes multiple concepts. It is not evidence that features are 1-D directions. The finding is observed on its own terms, but no version names it.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: First-PC replacement reportedly causes only a negligible classification-accuracy drop, consistent with a useful single-direction approximation (R2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The first principal component explains 48.2 of the second-order-effect variance, so the variance measure does not show a nearly one-dimensional effect (R1).
